name: TPS54240DGQR
title: TPS54240: 2.5-A buck regulator for 3.5-V to 42-V inputs, with Eco-Mode light-load skipping
summary: A non-synchronous buck regulator for inputs from 3.5 V to 42 V that carries its own 200-mΩ high-side N-channel switch and boot diode and needs an outside catch diode; it delivers up to 2.5 A. It runs peak current-mode control at a fixed frequency set by one resistor from 100 kHz to 2.5 MHz, or locks to an outside clock from 300 kHz to 2.2 MHz, and drops to pulse skipping (Eco-Mode) at light load, drawing 138 µA unloaded and 1.3 µA when disabled. It has an adjustable UVLO on EN, a slow-start/tracking pin, an open-drain power-good output with UV and OV windows, frequency foldback and thermal shutdown. It comes in a 10-pin HVSSOP (DGQ) and a 10-pin 3 mm × 3 mm VSON (DRC), both with an exposed pad.
key_figures: 100 kHz to 2500 kHz (RT); 300 kHz to 2200 kHz (CLK)
HVSSOP-10 (DGQ), VSON-10 3 mm × 3 mm (DRC), both with PowerPAD

notes: The orderable numbers differ in package (DGQ is the 10-pin HVSSOP, DRC the 10-pin 3 mm × 3 mm VSON), packing quantity and carrier, and lead finish.
An automotive-qualified version, TPS54240-Q1, exists as a separate device.
Both packages have a 3.00 mm × 3.00 mm nominal body.

pins.name: BOOT
pins.function: Bootstrap supply for the high-side gate drive; it takes a capacitor to PH. When its voltage falls below what the switch needs, the switch is held off until the capacitor has been recharged.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable, with an internal pull-up current source. Left open the part runs; below 1.2 V it is off. Two resistors on this pin set the input UVLO start and stop levels.

pins.name: SS/TR
pins.function: Slow-start and tracking. A capacitor to ground sets the output rise time; because the pin voltage takes the place of the internal reference while it is the lower of the two, it also serves for tracking and sequencing.

pins.name: RT/CLK
pins.function: Timing resistor or clock input. With a resistor to ground an internal amplifier holds the pin at a fixed voltage and the resistor sets the frequency. Driven above the PLL upper threshold, the amplifier turns off and the pin becomes a high-impedance clock input to the PLL; when clock edges stop, resistor mode returns.

pins.name: PWRGD
pins.function: Power-good output, open drain. Pulled low when the output is out of its window (undervoltage or overvoltage), in thermal shutdown, in dropout, or when EN shuts the part down.

pins.name: VSENSE
pins.function: Feedback input: the inverting node of the gm error amplifier.

pins.name: COMP
pins.function: Error-amplifier output and input to the switch-current comparator; the frequency-compensation network goes on this pin.

pins.name: PH
pins.function: Switch node, the source terminal of the built-in high-side power switch.

pins.name: POWERPAD
pins.function: Exposed pad. The GND pin must be tied to it on the board for the part to work correctly.

circuits.title: 3.3-V output design example
circuits.description: A 12-V nominal (10.8 V to 13.2 V) to 3.3-V, 2.5-A buck switching at 300 kHz. R3 (412 kΩ) sets the frequency; R1 and R2 on EN make it start at 6.25 V and stop at 5.9 V rising and falling; C3 sets slow start; R5 and R6 divide the output to the 0.8-V reference; R4 and C5 form the type 2A compensation, with C8 left open. C4 is the boot capacitor and D1 the outside catch diode.
notes: Board area for this design is about 0.55 in², test points and connectors not counted.

circuits.title: Inverting power supply
circuits.description: The buck runs with its ground pin on the negative output, so a positive input gives a negative output. Lo returns to system ground; the catch diode's anode, the divider foot and the IC's ground, slow-start, timing and compensation parts all sit on VOUT. Cd bypasses VIN to the IC ground; Cin bypasses VIN to system ground.
notes: EN is left open, so the part is enabled. PWRGD is not used. The exposed pad belongs with the IC's GND pin, which in this circuit is the VOUT node.
TI application report SLVA317 covers this design in more detail.

circuits.title: Split rail power supply
circuits.description: A coupled inductor turns the buck into a positive and negative supply. The IC's ground sits on the negative output VONEG; the main winding of Lo runs from PH to system ground, and the second winding, through its own diode, charges Copos to give VOPOS. R1 and R2 sense from VOPOS to VONEG.

parts.note: coupled inductor: winding 1 is pins 1-2 (dot at 1), winding 2 is pins 3-4 (dot at 4)

notes: EN is left open and PWRGD is not used. The exposed pad belongs with the IC's GND pin, which in this circuit is VONEG.
TI application report SLVA369 covers this design in more detail.

circuits.title: 12-V to 3.8-V GSM power supply
circuits.description: A buck for GSM-GPRS modules, which need a supply that rides out large load-current steps: 12 V nominal (8 V to 40 V) in, 3.8 V at 2.0 A out. R5 (237 kΩ) sets the frequency, R1 and R4 set the EN undervoltage levels, R2 and R6 set the output, and R3, C8 and C6 compensate the loop.
notes: PWRGD is left unconnected.
TI application report SLVA412 covers these GSM-GPRS supplies in more detail.

circuits.title: 24-V to 4.2-V GSM power supply
circuits.description: The same GSM-GPRS supply arranged for 24 V nominal (18 V to 40 V) in and 4.2 V at 2.0 A out, with R4 at 23.2 kΩ, a single 100-µF output capacitor, a 42.2-kΩ upper feedback resistor and a 4700-pF compensation capacitor.
notes: PWRGD is left unconnected.
TI application report SLVA412 covers these GSM-GPRS supplies in more detail.

circuits.title: Adjustable undervoltage lockout
circuits.description: R1 from VIN to EN and R2 from EN to ground set the input start and stop voltages, working against the 0.9-µA EN pull-up and the 2.9-µA hysteresis current added once EN passes 1.25 V (equations 2 and 3).
notes: The circuit uses only VIN and EN of the IC.

circuits.title: Adding additional hysteresis
circuits.description: The UVLO divider of R1 and R2 with a third resistor, R3, from the regulator output into EN; it adds hysteresis current, for a wider hysteresis or where the two-resistor values come out too high (equations 4 and 5).
notes: The circuit uses only VIN and EN of the IC.

circuits.title: Sequential startup sequence
circuits.description: Two regulators started one after the other: the open-drain PWRGD of the first drives EN of the second, so the second starts once the first is in regulation. Each has its own slow-start capacitor. A 1-nF ceramic capacitor on the second EN gives about 1 ms of extra delay if wanted.
notes: The circuit uses only EN, SS/TR and PWRGD of each IC.

circuits.title: Ratio-metric startup sequence
circuits.description: Two regulators with EN tied together and SS/TR tied together on one slow-start capacitor, so their outputs rise together and reach regulation at the same moment. Equation 6 is used with the charge current doubled.
notes: The circuit uses only EN, SS/TR and PWRGD of each IC.

circuits.title: Ratio-metric and simultaneous startup sequence
circuits.description: Two buck regulators with EN tied together. The first starts on its own slow-start capacitor C1; R1 and R2 divide its output VOUT1 into SS/TR of the second, so VOUT2 tracks VOUT1. R3 and R4 set VOUT2. R1 and R2 come from equations 7 to 10: deltaV of zero gives a simultaneous start, a positive deltaV a ratio-metric start with VOUT2 slightly below VOUT1, a negative one with VOUT2 slightly above.
notes: The circuit uses only EN, SS/TR, BOOT, PH, PWRGD and, on U2, VSENSE of each IC.

circuits.title: Synchronizing to a system clock
circuits.description: An outside clock reaches RT/CLK through a 10-pF capacitor and a 4-kΩ series resistor, while the frequency-set resistor Rfset runs from RT/CLK to the clock node, which is held to ground by 50 Ω, so Rfset still sets the frequency if the clock stops. Rfset is chosen to give a frequency near the clock's.
notes: The circuit uses only RT/CLK of the IC.

operation.text: Fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. The oscillator turns the high-side switch on each cycle; it turns off when the switch current reaches the level the COMP voltage asks for. COMP moves up and down with load current. Clamping COMP at a maximum gives the current limit; a minimum clamp gives Eco-Mode. A compensating ramp added to the sensed current stops subharmonic oscillation, and the peak current available stays the same across the whole duty-cycle range.

When the output is regulated and a cycle ends with peak switch current below the skip threshold (the current that matches a nominal 500 mV on COMP), the part stops switching and COMP is held at 500 mV. The output sags, COMP rises, and switching resumes on the next cycle until the peak current falls below the threshold again. Because peak current is what is sensed, the load at which skipping starts depends on the inductor; the 3.3-V example enters it near 5 mA. While idle the part draws 138 µA; the PLL keeps running, and with an outside clock the skip pulses stay in step with it.

The boot regulator and its diode are inside; a 0.1-µF ceramic capacitor (X5R or X7R, 10 V or more) from BOOT to PH supplies the high-side gate, recharged while the catch diode conducts. The switch may stay on at 100% duty as long as BOOT-PH stays above 2.1 V; below that a UVLO turns it off so the capacitor can recharge. Since little current is drawn from the boot capacitor, the switch can stay on for many cycles. At light or no load near dropout the inductor current may be too small to drag PH low and recharge the capacitor, so switching stops until VIN − VOUT exceeds about 2.1 V. Setting the VIN stop voltage with the EN divider above this point avoids it. Ripple grows at very high duty because the boot recharge time exceeds the normal off-time.

operation.topic: Start and stop voltages near dropout
operation.text: The start voltage is the input needed to bring the output within 1% of its setting; the stop voltage is the input at which the output falls 5% or switching stops. Both depend on load current.

A transconductance amplifier compares VSENSE with whichever is lower, SS/TR or the 0.8-V reference. Its gm is 310 µA/V normally and 70 µA/V while VSENSE is under 0.8 V and the part regulates to SS/TR. The compensation network goes from COMP to ground.
A bandgap-based reference, scaled to 0.8 V, held within ±2% over temperature.

A divider from the output to VSENSE sets the output (equation 1). Larger values improve light-load efficiency, but too large makes the loop sensitive to noise and lets the VSENSE input current cause errors; keep at least 1 µA in the divider, which limits the lower resistor to 800 kΩ.

The part shuts off when VIN falls below 2.5 V. EN has a 0.9-µA pull-up, so the part runs with EN open; once EN exceeds 1.25 V a further 2.9 µA is added, which gives hysteresis. Two resistors set the start and stop input voltages (equations 2 and 3); this is not required but is strongly advised for repeatable power-up. A third resistor from the output into EN widens the hysteresis (equations 4 and 5). With EN below about 1.2 V the part is off and draws its least current; it becomes active when both EN and VIN are above their thresholds, then begins switching with a slow start.

The part is specified from 3.5 V, but may run down to the 2.5-V UVLO level; below UVLO it does not switch. With EN open or pulled up by a divider from VIN, it becomes active once VIN passes UVLO and starts with the slow-start ramp.

The error amplifier uses the lower of SS/TR and the internal reference. A 2-µA source charges the capacitor on SS/TR, so the capacitor sets the start-up time (equation 6). At power-up switching does not start until SS/TR has been discharged below 40 mV; the same discharge happens after a UVLO trip, EN pulled below 1.25 V, or thermal shutdown. Until SS/TR reaches 85% of the reference, VSENSE tracks it 45 mV apart; above that the offset grows as control passes to the internal reference, which is complete once SS/TR is above 1.3 V. SS/TR ramps linearly until it is clamped at 1.7 V.
When a fault drives the error amplifier high, a 382-µA pull-down brings SS/TR down to just above VSENSE. When the fault is removed the output ramps back up from wherever it fell, as in a slow start.

Sequential start: PWRGD of one regulator (or any open-drain reset output) drives EN of the next, so the second starts when the first is in regulation; 1 nF on the second EN adds about 1 ms of delay. Ratio-metric start: SS/TR pins tied together make both outputs rise and arrive together, with the charge current doubled in equation 6. Ratio-metric or simultaneous tracking: a divider (R1, R2) from the leading output into SS/TR of the following regulator, sized by equations 7 to 9; deltaV is zero for simultaneous start, negative to have the second output finish slightly above the first. R1 must exceed equation 10 so the part can restart after a fault.

A resistor from RT/CLK to ground, where the pin sits near 0.5 V, sets the frequency from about 100 kHz to 2500 kHz (equation 11). Higher frequency means smaller parts, but efficiency, the highest input voltage and the 135-ns typical minimum on-time limit it; frequency-shift protection limits it further.

The switch is turned off each cycle when its current meets the COMP level. In overload the output falls, COMP rises to its internal clamp, and that clamp is the switch current limit. To keep control of inductor current in a short at high input, the frequency is divided by 8, 4, 2 and 1 as VSENSE rises from 0 to 0.8 V, which lengthens the off-time so the current can ramp down. The division is digital so that it also works while synchronized to a clock. Because 8 is the largest divider, there is a highest input voltage at which this protection still holds.

Use the lower of equation 12 (the limit set by minimum on-time, above which pulses are skipped) and equation 13 (the limit for short-circuit protection with frequency shift, where fdiv goes from 1 to 8 as the output falls to zero).

A square wave on RT/CLK going below 0.5 V and above 2.2 V, high and low for more than 40 ns each, between 300 kHz and 2200 kHz, synchronizes the part; the PH rising edge follows the clock's falling edge. Couple it through 10 pF and 4 kΩ and keep the frequency-set resistor, returned through 50 Ω to ground, set close to the clock frequency so the part carries on if the clock stops. The series resistor cuts PH jitter at heavy load and on the change back to resistor mode. On the first clock edge above threshold the 0.5-V source is removed, the pin goes high impedance, and the PLL locks within 100 µs, up or down from the resistor frequency. If the clock stops, the frequency falls to 150 kHz, the 0.5 V returns and the resistor takes over again. Synchronization holds in continuous, discontinuous and pulse-skip operation.

PWRGD is open drain. It is released when VSENSE is between 94% and 107% of the reference, and pulled low below 92% or above 109%, during UVLO or thermal shutdown, or with EN low. A pull-up of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ to 5.5 V or less is advised. Its state is defined once VIN exceeds 1.5 V, with full sinking ability as VIN nears 3 V.

After an overload or a sharp load release, the output can rise faster than the error amplifier can come back down, especially with a small output capacitor. When VSENSE goes above 109% of the reference the high-side switch is held off; it may turn on again on the next cycle after VSENSE falls below that level.
Above 182 °C junction the part stops switching. Once it cools below 182 °C it starts again with a full power-up sequence, discharging SS/TR first.

For simulation, the error amplifier is a voltage-controlled current source of 310 µA/V with Ro and Co setting its open-loop gain and bandwidth; the power stage is a 10.5-A/V transconductance from COMP to switch current. This model holds in continuous conduction only. The control-to-output response has a dc gain, one pole that moves with load, and the ESR zero (equations 14 to 17); as load falls the gain rises and the pole drops, so the crossover stays roughly fixed. High-ESR electrolytic capacitors can reduce the compensation parts needed.

Three networks from COMP to ground suit the gm amplifier: type 2A (series R3–C1 with C2 in parallel), type 2B (series R3–C1 only) and type 1 (C2 only). The type 2 networks suit wide-bandwidth designs with low-ESR output capacitors; type 1 suits high-ESR electrolytic or tantalum output capacitors (equations 18 to 27).

Size it with equation 28. Ripple current must be filtered by, and within the ripple rating of, the output capacitor. Keep ripple above 150 mA; with a wide input range lean toward more ripple so it stays measurable at low input. Since the inductor current can reach the switch current limit during start-up, faults or transients, the safest choice is a saturation rating at or above the current limit. In the 3.3-V example KIND = 0.3 gives 11 µH, 10 µH is used, the RMS current is 2.51 A and the peak 2.913 A.

Three limits apply and the strictest wins: holding the output through a load step for about two cycles until the loop responds (equation 32), absorbing inductor energy on load release since the catch diode cannot sink current (equation 33), and the ripple (equations 34 and 35). Allow for ageing, temperature and dc-bias derating. In the 3.3-V example these give 67 µF, 60 µF and 12 µF, with ESR under 36 mΩ; two 47-µF 10-V ceramics (3 mΩ, 72.4 µF after derating) are used, and the ripple current is 238 mA (equation 36).

An outside diode goes from PH to GND, rated for at least the highest input voltage in reverse and above the peak inductor current, with low forward voltage; Schottky types fit. At higher frequency the junction capacitance and recovery losses add to conduction loss (equation 37). The example uses a B360B-13-F (60 V, 0.70 V typical forward drop, 200 pF), dissipating 1.32 W. Where the supply spends long periods at light load or asleep, a diode with lower leakage and slightly higher forward drop may be preferred.

At least 3 µF of effective X5R or X7R ceramic capacitance, counting dc-bias loss, rated above the highest input voltage and for the input ripple current (equation 38); bulk capacitance may be added. Input ripple follows equation 39. The example uses two 2.2-µF 100-V capacitors (4.4 µF), giving 206 mV of ripple and 1.15 A RMS ripple current.

Slow start has to last long enough that charging the output capacitance needs no excessive current (equation 40), which avoids hitting current limit or pulling the input down. The example needs 0.19 ms to charge 72.4 µF at 1 A average; it uses 3.5 ms, needing 8.75 nF, rounded up to 10 nF.

With 13.2 V maximum input the skip limit is 2247 kHz; with a 0.7-V diode, 26 mΩ inductor, 200 mΩ switch, 3.5-A current limit and 0.2 V output in a short, the shift limit is about 4449 kHz. 300 kHz is used, set by 412 kΩ. The EN divider is 124 kΩ (VIN to EN) and 30.1 kΩ (EN to ground) for 6.25-V start and 5.9-V stop. The feedback lower resistor is 10.0 kΩ; equation 1 gives 31.25 kΩ, rounded to 31.6 kΩ.

The method ignores the internal slope compensation, so the real crossover tends to come out lower than calculated, and assumes the crossover lies between the modulator pole and an ESR zero at least ten times higher. With a derated 40 µF, the modulator pole is 1206 Hz and the ESR zero 530.5 kHz; equations 43 and 44 give 25.3 kHz and 13.4 kHz, and 35.0 kHz is chosen for faster transients. R4 comes to 20.2 kΩ (20.0 kΩ used) and C5 to 4740 pF (4700 pF used); the optional pole capacitor C8 is not fitted.
At 12 V in, the supply goes discontinuous below 337 mA of load and into Eco-Mode below 5 mA; with no load it draws 392 µA from the input.

IC loss is conduction plus switching plus gate drive plus supply current (equations 49 to 53), valid in continuous conduction only; junction and highest ambient temperatures follow from the package thermal resistance (equations 54 and 55). Inductor, diode and trace losses come on top.
The input supply should be well regulated, between 3.5 V and 42 V. If it is more than a few inches away, add bulk capacitance beside the ceramics; 100 µF electrolytic is typical.

Bypass VIN to ground with a low-ESR X5R or X7R ceramic and keep the loop through the bypass capacitor, VIN and the catch diode anode small. Tie GND straight to the exposed pad, and the pad to inner ground planes through several vias beneath the IC. PH is the switching node: route it to the diode cathode and the inductor, keep both close, and keep its copper area small to limit capacitive coupling. At full load the top-side ground must provide enough area to spread heat. RT/CLK picks up noise easily, so place the RT resistor close to the IC with short traces. The boot capacitor trace can be routed on another layer to leave a wide top-side ground path.

packages.name: DGQ0010D (HVSSOP-10 PowerPAD)
rows: span from pin 1 to pin 5 centres (2X)
exposed thermal pad, along the leads
land: thermal pad solder mask opening
solder mask clearance, non solder mask defined
solder mask overlap, solder mask defined
notes: Same body and flash limits as DGQ0010H, JEDEC MO-187 variation BA-T; this outline has a smaller, squarer exposed pad.

packages.name: DRC0010J (VSON-10, 3 mm × 3 mm)
rows: span from pin 1 to pin 5 centres (2X)
land: thermal pad length including its tabs
solder mask clearance, non solder mask defined (preferred)
solder mask overlap, solder mask defined
notes: The thermal pad must be soldered to the board for best thermal and mechanical performance.
The stencil example is for a 0.125 mm stencil and prints 80% of the thermal pad area. Vias in the pad are optional; vias under paste should be filled, plugged or tented.
